T₉ = C(8, 8) (3x)^(8−8) (−1/(2x))⁸

Work out each factor's remainder separately, using the fact that powers repeat in a cycle
modulo 5.
**Step 1 — 3¹⁰⁰ mod 5.** The powers of 3 cycle with period 4:
3¹ ≡ 3, 3² ≡ 4, 3³ ≡ 2, **3⁴ ≡ 81 ≡ 1** (mod 5)
Since 100 = 4 × 25,
3¹⁰⁰ = (3⁴)²⁵ ≡ 1²⁵ = **1** (mod 5)
**Step 2 — 2⁵⁰ mod 5.** The powers of 2 also cycle with period 4:
2¹ ≡ 2, 2² ≡ 4, 2³ ≡ 3, **2⁴ ≡ 16 ≡ 1** (mod 5)
Since 50 = 4 × 12 + 2,
2⁵⁰ = (2⁴)¹² × 2² ≡ 1 × 4 = **4** (mod 5)
**Step 3 — multiply the remainders.**
3¹⁰⁰ × 2⁵⁰ ≡ 1 × 4 = **4** (mod 5) ✓
The principle that makes this work is that remainders **multiply**: if a ≡ p and b ≡ q, then
ab ≡ pq. So the two huge powers can be reduced separately and the small results combined.
The period of 4 in both cases is no accident — it is **Fermat's little theorem**, which says
a⁴ ≡ 1 (mod 5) for any a not divisible by 5. Knowing that, the only work is reducing the
exponents 100 and 50 modulo 4, giving 0 and 2.
∴ 4.

kcet|Mathematics|2011|15|MTG Karnataka-C:
Write the two terms out and set them equal.
**Step 1 — the general term.** In (p + q)ⁿ,
T_r = C(n, r−1) p^(n−r+1) q^(r−1)
T_(r+1) = C(n, r) p^(n−r) q^r
**Step 2 — equate them.**
C(n, r−1) p^(n−r+1) q^(r−1) = C(n, r) p^(n−r) q^r
Divide both sides by p^(n−r) q^(r−1), which cancels most of the powers:
C(n, r−1) · **p** = C(n, r) · **q**
**Step 3 — use the ratio of the binomial coefficients.** A standard identity gives
C(n, r) / C(n, r−1) = (n − r + 1) / r
So
p / q = C(n, r)/C(n, r−1) = (n − r + 1)/r
**r p = (n − r + 1) q**
**Step 4 — rearrange into the required form.**
rp = nq − rq + q
rp + rq = nq + q
**r(p + q) = (n + 1) q**
Therefore
**(n + 1)q / [r(p + q)] = 1** ✓
The expression in the question is not arbitrary — it has been built so that the condition
for two consecutive terms to be equal rearranges into exactly that ratio. Recognising that
the algebra is meant to collapse to 1 is itself a hint, and it is worth carrying the
rearrangement all the way rather than stopping at r p = (n − r + 1) q.
∴ 1.

kcet|Mathematics|2013|22|MTG Karnataka-C:
Let **a** be composite and let **p** be its smallest divisor greater than 1.
**Step 1 — p is prime.** If p had a divisor d with 1 < d < p, then d would also divide a and
would be smaller than p — contradicting the choice of p as the **smallest**. So p is prime.
**Step 2 — write a = p · q.** Since a is composite, it has such a factorisation with q > 1,
and q is itself a divisor of a greater than 1.
**Step 3 — compare p with q.** Because p is the **smallest** divisor above 1,
**p ≤ q**
**Step 4 — multiply that inequality by p.**
p² ≤ pq = a
Taking the square root,
**p ≤ √a** ✓ — option (d)
**When is equality reached?** When p = q, that is when a is the square of a prime: for
a = 9, p = 3 = √9; for a = 49, p = 7 = √49. So p can **equal** √a, which is why the answer
uses **≤** and not the strict **<** of option (a).
Two quick illustrations: for a = 15, p = 3 and √15 ≈ 3·87, so 3 < 3·87 ✓; for a = 25, p = 5
and √25 = 5, so equality ✓
This result is the basis of the standard **primality test**: to decide whether a number is
prime it is enough to try dividing it by every prime up to √a, since a composite number must
have a factor there.
∴ ≤ √a.

(−2ω)⁶ = 64 ω⁶ = 64 (ω³)² = 64 × 1 = **64**

**Step 4 — subtract.**
64 − 64 = **0** ✓

The surprise of this question is that **i^i is a real number**, so its imaginary part is
zero.
**Step 1 — write i in exponential form.** On the unit circle, i has modulus 1 and argument
π/2:
**i = e^(iπ/2)**
**Step 2 — raise it to the power i.**
i^i = (e^(iπ/2))^i = e^(i · iπ/2) = e^(i² π/2)
**Step 3 — use i² = −1.**
= **e^(−π/2)**
**Step 4 — read off the parts.** e^(−π/2) ≈ e^(−1·5708) ≈ **0·2079**, a plain positive real
number. Its **imaginary part is 0** ✓
So raising an imaginary number to an imaginary power produces something real — one of the
more startling identities in elementary complex analysis, and a cousin of Euler's
e^(iπ) + 1 = 0.
One refinement is worth mentioning: the argument of i is π/2 **plus any multiple of 2π**, so
strictly i^i has infinitely many values, e^(−π/2 + 2kπ) for integer k. Every one of them is
real, so the imaginary part is zero whichever branch is taken — the answer does not depend
on the choice.
The **principal value** is the one with k = 0, namely e^(−π/2).
∴ 0.

Use the two properties of the cube roots of unity:
**ω³ = 1**  and  **1 + ω + ω² = 0**, from which **1 + ω = −ω²** and **1 + ω² = −ω**
**Step 1 — reduce the higher powers.** Since ω³ = 1, exponents can be taken modulo 3:
ω⁴ = ω³·ω = **ω**
ω⁸ = ω⁶·ω² = (ω³)²·ω² = **ω²**
So the product becomes
(1 + ω)(1 + ω²)(1 + ω)(1 + ω²)
**Step 2 — substitute.**
= (−ω²)(−ω)(−ω²)(−ω)
**Step 3 — multiply.** Four minus signs give a plus:
= ω² · ω · ω² · ω = **ω⁶**
**Step 4 — reduce.**
ω⁶ = (ω³)² = 1² = **1** ✓

(−ω²)(−ω) = ω³ = **1**, so the whole product is 1 × 1 = 1.
The step that must not be skipped is **reducing ω⁴ and ω⁸ first**. Without it the expression
looks like four different factors, and the symmetry that makes the answer so clean is
hidden. Exponent arithmetic modulo 3 is the single technique this whole family of questions
rests on.

Let θ = π/8 and write the numerator as **z**. Then the denominator is exactly its
**conjugate** z̄, since the two differ only in the sign of the imaginary part:
z = (1 + sin θ) + i cos θ
z̄ = (1 + sin θ) − i cos θ
**Step 1 — simplify z/z̄.** For any complex number, z/z̄ has modulus 1 and argument twice
that of z:
**z/z̄ = e^(2i·arg z)**
**Step 2 — find arg z.**
tan(arg z) = cos θ / (1 + sin θ)
There is a standard identity for this:
cos θ / (1 + sin θ) = **tan(π/4 − θ/2)**
So with θ = π/8,
arg z = π/4 − π/16 = **3π/16**
**Step 3 — form the nth power.**
(z/z̄)ⁿ = e^(2in · 3π/16) = e^(i · 3πn/8)
**Step 4 — impose 'purely imaginary'.** A complex number of modulus 1 is purely imaginary
when its argument is an odd multiple of π/2:
3πn/8 = π/2 + kπ
3n/8 = 1/2 + k
3n = 4 + 8k
Try k = 0, 1, 2, …: 3n = 4 ✗, 3n = 12 ⟹ **n = 4** ✓
So the smallest positive integer is **4**.
The identity in step 2 is the crux, and it is worth deriving once: writing
cos θ = cos²(θ/2) − sin²(θ/2) and 1 + sin θ = (cos(θ/2) + sin(θ/2))², the fraction reduces to
(cos(θ/2) − sin(θ/2))/(cos(θ/2) + sin(θ/2)), which is tan(π/4 − θ/2).
∴ 4.

kcet|Mathematics|2006|9|MTG Karnataka-CE.s:
The locus of a point whose distances from two fixed points are in a **constant ratio** is a
**circle** — the **circle of Apollonius** ✓.
**The derivation.** Put the two fixed points at A(a, 0) and B(−a, 0), and let P(x, y) satisfy
PA/PB = K. Squaring,
PA² = K² PB²
(x − a)² + y² = K²[(x + a)² + y²]
x² − 2ax + a² + y² = K²x² + 2aK²x + K²a² + K²y²
Collecting terms,
(1 − K²)x² + (1 − K²)y² − 2a(1 + K²)x + a²(1 − K²) = 0
Divide through by (1 − K²), which is non-zero because **K < 1**:
x² + y² − [2a(1 + K²)/(1 − K²)]x + a² = 0
The coefficients of x² and y² are **equal** and there is no xy term, so this is the equation
of a **circle** ✓
**The special case.** If K = 1 the division is impossible — and indeed the x² and y² terms
cancel, leaving x = 0, the **perpendicular bisector** of AB. So the locus is a straight line
only when the distances are equal, which the condition K < 1 excludes.
Why the other conics do not arise: an **ellipse** is the locus of constant **sum** of
distances from two points, a **hyperbola** the locus of constant **difference**. A constant
**ratio** gives a circle. The ratio definition does produce a conic — but only when it is
measured from a point and a **line** (the focus-directrix property), not from two points.
∴ circle.

Note: the printed key gives (b), ellipse. An ellipse is the locus of constant *sum* of
distances; a constant *ratio* gives the Apollonius circle, so the key is wrong and has been
corrected to (d).
